item.title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour
item.description:
Source: www.nature.com

https://archive.ph/zIPG4

Top Comment:

Coral gets its color from algae called zooxanthellae, which it depends on for photosynthesis.

Bleaching is actually due to the coral expelling those algae. Bleached corals are not dead, and remarkably they can not only let the algae in again but can also select a different algae species to cultivate (changing colour in the process)!.

This is thought to be a deliberate survival strategy to optimize the species of algae under different conditions (Adaptive Bleaching Hypothesis).

Bleaching is caused by the same stressors (like high temperature) which kill coral, but bleaching itself is not death of the coral.

item.description:

Top Comment:

I feel like we're reliving the late 1790s again, back then you had Ramsden figuring out how to divide the circle into into seconds of arc, taking the marking of scales from an artform into something that could be manufactured reliably. Maudslay with his thread cutting lathe took the making of screws from a manual process pawned off on apprentices to something that that could be done in mass production. Wilkinson's boring machine made it possible for Watt to build a pressurized steam engine.

All of these tools are based on things that were one-offs of earlier efforts, and turned into practical machine tools by someone that history chose to remember. We're now at the point where making things by manipulating individual atoms is something a determined amateur can do, it's amazing!

I find myself fascinated by the Wyler Inclinometer, which uses a thin copper disk with spiral arms as the basis of a differential capacitor, and when complete, resulting in a device that can used to calibrate a granite surface plate. It can typically measure 1 micron/meter of deviation.

We now have 3d printers that can reliably make almost anything you want by fusing filament, or stereolithography, or fusion of metal powders. You can buy desktop 5 axis CNC machines. There are control systems available to let you build almost any type of machine tool you can imagine, in as many axis as you want.

We've got software defined radio, cheap atomic clocks, transistors that can switch megawatts, all within reach of a hobbyist.

What an amazing time to be alive.

item.title: Parser Combinators
item.description:
Source: t3.at

Top Comment:

If you're on Python and your problem is too big for a single regex, but too small for a full-blown parser like in the article, I can recommend the built-in re.Scanner[0]. It's a regex-based tokenizer[1] (so no recursive parsing) in the `re` module, that for reasons is completely missing from any official documentation.

You give it a pattern for each token type, and a function to process each match, and you get back a list of processed tokens.

Importantly, it processes the list in one pass and ensures the matches are contiguous, where a naive `re.findall` with capture groups will ignore unmatched characters. You also get a reference to the running scanner, so you can record the location of the match for reporting errors.

    import re

    # Initialize the scanner.
    scanner = re.Scanner([
      (r"\d+",   lambda scanner, token: ('COUNT', int(token))),
      (r"\w+",   lambda scanner, token: ('ANIMAL', token.removesuffix('s'))),
      (r"[,. ]",     None), # None -> skip token.
    ])

    # Scan a sample string.
    results, remainder = scanner.scan("45 pigeons, 23 cows, 11 spiders.")

    # Ensure we parsed the whole thing.
    assert not remainder

    print(results)
    # [('COUNT', 45),
    #  ('ANIMAL', 'pigeon'),
    #  ('COUNT', 23),
    #  ('ANIMAL', 'cow'),
    #  ('COUNT', 11),
    #  ('ANIMAL', 'spider')]
[0]: https://stackoverflow.com/a/693818/252218

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexical_analysis#Tokenization

item.title: Lean now ships with verified kernels
item.description:
Source: leodemoura.github.io

Top Comment:

Suppose lean in its current state existed 15 years ago, and suppose the math community eagerly started contributing en masse to a shared repository of code. How much of the breakthroughs and longstanding questions in mathematics that we’ve seen answered this year do you think we would have solved?

In other words, how much of the developments this year are directly attributable to LLMs using lean, versus lean just being a significantly more productive language for some subset of mathematics compared to English and LaTeX?

Given how much we’ve seen formalized this year it feels hard to believe that this couldn’t have happened earlier.

Follow up question: do you think mathematicians would be as upset about the rapid changes in their field if they were the result of a collective shared effort on github, authored entirely by humans who all share the credit, versus that same outcome but authored by a large language model?

In other words, are the mathematicians upset about large language models, or are they really just upset that formalization and massive collaboration have turned out to be highly effective and has negated the heroic angle that mathematicians previously enjoyed, thinking in a locked room by themselves?

Food for thought.

A coworker recently remarked that lean seems like a new foundational language family that every programmer should be able to read, on par with C and Python, and I think it’s pretty hard to disagree with that. Next generations of models are going to be RL’d on Lean more and more because it pays dividends in winning the math war against their competitors, and this will benefit users of lean not only for mathematics but also as a general programming language and as a vehicle for other DSLs. For example, I think Sparkle (a Lean based HDL) or something like it makes a lot of sense in 2026 and beyond.

item.title: Codex Desktop continuously generates Crashpad pending dumps
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

I'd been running into a lot of disk pressure on my system from agents running. I discovered two main causes:

- my approach to using git worktrees for all work. Not entirely surprising, the duplicated build artifacts in each worktree being the main culprit here. There were some limited gains to be had by just being more efficient with how builds were managed but ultimately I just had to limit the number of concurrent features I was working on in a couple of particularly large repos.

- more insidious was the fact I was actually hitting memory limits more than I realised and causing my mac to have to swap heavily. The system was surprisingly still quite performant while this was happening... until it wasn't. Unfortunately as best I can tell the only "fix" when this happens is to restart the machine. There's no way to have the system reclaim any of the swap space once it's written to disk. Which if you have it thrash a couple of times a day (especially easy if you leave something running overnight) adds up very quickly.

item.description:
Source: legendofhyrule.com

I made this ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake which comes out in 17 days. I remember the feeling of playing it as a kid but I hadn’t kept up with the story so I built a timeline to catch up before the Door of Time reopens.

Nintendo’s own timeline is the authority here (Hyrule Historia and their chronicle page). The fun part was rethinking how to visualize it. It branches at the end of Ocarina into three eras depending on whether Link wins or loses, so each era is its own thread on the cloth. The threads meet again much later with Breath of the Wild.

I had a lot of help from Claude. I’d often thought about building things like this but never found the time between the day job and the rest of life.

Top Comment:

I don't consider it to be one unified story at all, I mean some of the series obviously are connected, but the rest are, as the name suggests, legends about Zelda. Unconnected unreliable narrations about some sort of heroic past events. Everybody agrees about the characters involved but as to what exactly happened, that is lost to time. So each culture is now telling the story a different way, emphasizing whatever is important to them.

I consider as a sort of modern equivalent to the coyote stories. or Paul Bunyan, Finn McCool, Gilgamesh, Or really, any legendary heroic epic passed along by oral storytelling.

So it is fun to try to fit it into some sort of unified timeline. But I don't think it is, that is not how they were actually written and we would loose most of the interesting storytelling flexibility if that is how they write them in the future.

item.title: Florida's HOAs and condo associations are making the housing crisis worse
item.description:
Source: hoaspy.com

Top Comment:

(My comment is about detached houses).

I (thankfully) live in a neighborhood without an HOA. Just one block away, there is an HOA. No reason to prefer that street (and home values aren't higher there).

This isn't an upper class neighborhood. It's mixed. Half of the residents are blue collar workers.

Over the years, I would think of reasons/annoyances where I'd say "Yes, while I'm glad I don't have an HOA, if we did have one it would take care of this or that annoying problem with the neighbor."

Then I spoke to friends who live in HOA neighborhoods and are on the HOA board. They told me clearly that "No, in practice, the HOA is not going to get involved in those (serious) matters. All they care about is the veneer (house appearance) and really petty rules." They also told me the purpose of the HOA was to justify its own existence. The owners get almost nothing for the funds they collect, other than a 3rd party company driving by and noting minor violations.

Another friend just had to spend $4000 to paint the front of his house. He's temporarily living in another state for a work assignment, and he and several others got notices that the HOA has decided to change the "look" of the neighborhood. Otherwise his house looked fine (not worn out paint or anything). I bet someone in the neighborhood has friends with a painting outfit.

I can stomach the idea of an HOA if they solved real problems (sanitation, etc), and not just appearances, but they don't. Even if it's in their bylaws, they don't enforce the serious stuff. Just the petty stuff.

Someone losing a home because they decided to have a window AC facing the street is plain immoral.
